alt: Drawing of a simple calorimeter made from two nested foam cups, labeled Styrofoam cups, holding a blue liquid labeled reaction mixture. A cover sits on top. A thermometer, with its red liquid column, passes through the cover into the liquid, and a wire loop stirrer, with a double arrow showing it moves up and down, also passes through the cover.
caption: A coffee-cup calorimeter: two nested foam cups, a cover, a thermometer, and a stirrer. The foam and cover keep heat from escaping, so the heat lost by one part of the contents equals the heat gained by the other. This is the setup used in Experiment 7a.
why: The section and Lab 7a use a foam-cup calorimeter but never show one; labeled apparatus diagram.

lead: Boiling points show how much hydrogen bonding adds. The graph below plots the boiling points of the simple hydrogen compounds of Groups 15, 16, and 17. From period 3 down, each group’s boiling point rises as the molecules get more electrons, the dispersion trend from earlier in this section. The period 2 compounds, NH3, H2O, and HF, break the pattern: they hydrogen bond, so they boil far higher than the trend predicts.
alt: Line graph of boiling point in degrees Celsius, from minus 150 to 150, versus period, 2 to 5, for three groups of hydrogen compounds. Group 16, blue: H2O about 100, H2S about minus 60, H2Se about minus 41, H2Te about 0. Group 17, orange: HF about 20, HCl about minus 85, HBr about minus 67, HI about minus 35. Group 15, green: NH3 about minus 33, PH3 about minus 88, AsH3 about minus 62, SbH3 about minus 17. Each line dips from period 2 to period 3 and then rises steadily through periods 4 and 5; H2O, HF, and NH3 sit far above where the trend from the heavier compounds would put them.
caption: Boiling points of the hydrogen compounds of Groups 15–17. Below period 2 the boiling point rises with the number of electrons. H<sub>2</sub>O, HF, and NH<sub>3</sub> are far higher than the trend predicts because their molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
why: Real data graph that makes the hydrogen-bonding boiling-point anomaly visible; gives ready rank-by-boiling-point practice.

key: The two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds between base pairs
alt: Structural drawing of a short piece of double-stranded DNA. A sugar-phosphate backbone runs down each side, and the bases in the middle pair up across the gap. Thymine pairs with adenine through two dotted lines labeled hydrogen bonds, from N–H to N and from N–H to O. Guanine pairs with cytosine through three dotted hydrogen bonds, each between an N–H and an O or N. The strand ends are labeled 5 prime and 3 prime.
caption: Base pairs in DNA. Adenine and thymine are joined by two hydrogen bonds, and guanine and cytosine by three (dotted lines). Every hydrogen bond links an H on N to a lone pair on N or O, the FNO rule at work in a living cell.
why: Illustrates the Biology Connection box exactly (A-T two H bonds, G-C three) and reinforces the N/O/F donor-acceptor rule.

key: Capillary action is a liquid rising in a narrow tube
lead: Clinics use capillary action every day. For a fingerstick blood test, a health worker touches a thin glass capillary tube to the drop of blood. Adhesion between the blood, which is mostly water, and the glass draws the blood up the tube with no suction.
alt: Photograph of a fingerstick blood draw. A health worker in white gloves holds a patient’s fingertip, which has a small drop of red blood on it, and touches the end of a thin, clear tube to the drop. The lower part of the tube is filled with red blood.
caption: Collecting a blood sample by capillary action. Blood rises into the narrow tube because its attraction to the tube wall (adhesion) is stronger than its attraction to itself (cohesion).
credit_extra: photo: modification of work by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
why: Allied-health photo of capillary action, which the page defines only in words.

key: the powder has much more sur
lead: Iron shows the same surface-area effect. The photos below compare iron powder and an iron nail, each in dilute hydrochloric acid.
alt: Two photographs of test tubes. (a) Gray, cloudy liquid with dark iron powder at the bottom, covered in a thick layer of gas bubbles. (b) Clear, pale yellow-green liquid around an iron nail; only small bubbles cling along the nail.
caption: Surface area and rate. (a) Iron powder reacts quickly with dilute hydrochloric acid, giving off many bubbles of hydrogen gas. (b) An iron nail reacts much more slowly, because far fewer iron atoms are exposed to collisions with the acid.
why: Real lab photo for the surface-area factor, which our page shows only as particle art and a table row.

key: A good picture is a ski hill on a busy afternoon
lead: Two jugglers passing clubs back and forth show the same idea.
alt: Photograph of two young men in white T-shirts facing each other in an arched courtyard, juggling clubs between them. Several white and orange clubs are in the air between the two jugglers, and each man holds one or two clubs in his hands.
caption: A juggling picture of dynamic equilibrium. Each juggler throws and catches clubs at the same rate, so the number each one holds stays about the same even though the clubs never stop moving, just as the forward and reverse reactions keep running at equal rates.
why: A photo analogy for "dynamic" (constant amounts, nonstop motion) next to the ski-hill analogy.

lead: You hear a pressure shift every time you open a soda. Carbonated drinks are sealed under a high pressure of CO2, so a lot of CO2 dissolves: CO2(g) ⇄ CO2(aq). Opening the bottle lets gas escape and lowers the pressure above the drink. The equilibrium shifts toward the side with more moles of gas, so dissolved CO2 comes out of solution as bubbles.
alt: Close-up photograph of an opened bottle of cola held in a hand. A layer of tan foam and bubbles sits on top of the dark liquid. Drawn over the liquid are small carbon dioxide molecules, each a gray carbon between two red oxygens, with white curved arrows showing them rising out of the liquid into the bubbles.
caption: Opening a soft drink lowers the CO<sub>2</sub> pressure above it, so CO<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇄ CO<sub>2</sub>(aq) shifts toward the gas, and dissolved CO<sub>2</sub> escapes as bubbles. A soda left open goes flat.
credit_extra: photo: modification of work by “D Coetzee”/Flickr
why: Everyday photo of a Le Chatelier pressure shift (the main skill of the chapter).

key: Most nitrogen fertilizer, including much of what feeds Valley orchards
alt: Diagram of an industrial ammonia plant. Nitrogen and hydrogen feed gases enter through a compressor at upper left into a tall catalyst chamber, labeled 400 to 500 degrees Celsius, that contains a heater coil at the bottom, two catalyst layers, and a heat exchanger at the top. A pipe carrying NH3 and unreacted N2 and H2 runs from the chamber through a second heat exchanger to a condenser, where cold water flows in and hot water flows out around a coil. Below the condenser, refrigeration turns the ammonia into liquid NH3, which collects in a storage tank. A return pipe labeled recycled N2, H2 carries the unreacted gases back through a compressor into the catalyst chamber.
caption: An industrial Haber process plant for N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇄ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g). High pressure (fewer moles of gas on the product side) and removing NH<sub>3</sub> as a liquid in the condenser both shift the equilibrium toward ammonia. The catalyst does not shift it; it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster. Unreacted N<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> are recycled.
why: Shows every engineering choice in the Valley fertilizer box (pressure, catalyst, NH3 removal, recycling) on one diagram.
